note: Fixture set for the TTB label verification prototype. `application` is the typed-in half of the COLA application; `labelText` is ground truth for what the artwork actually prints (null means deliberately absent); `expected` is the verdict a correct implementation must reach. Check ids in `expected.checks` correspond to CheckResult.id in src/lib/ttb/rules.ts. Check ids match CheckResult.id in src/lib/ttb/rules.ts; see tests/samples.test.ts.

canonicalWarning.body: (1) According to the Surgeon General, women should not drink alcoholic beverages during pregnancy because of the risk of birth defects. (2) Consumption of alcoholic beverages impairs your ability to drive a car or operate machinery, and may cause health problems.

samples.title: Hollow Creek Vineyards — compliant wine
samples.description: Compliant wine label with a different layout and typographic voice from the spirits samples. The alcohol statement is printed in the trade format 'ALCOHOL 13.5% BY VOLUME' while the application records '13.5% Alc./Vol.'. That is a formatting difference, not a defect: a correct implementation normalises both to 13.5 and passes.

samples.title: Stone’s Throw — case and apostrophe variance (must PASS)
samples.description: Trap sample. The artwork sets the brand as 'STONE’S THROW' in display capitals with a typographic apostrophe (U+2019); the application types 'Stone's Throw' in title case with an ASCII apostrophe (U+0027). A correct implementation case-folds and unicode-normalises before comparing and returns PASS. Flagging this as a mismatch is a false positive and the single most likely defect in a naive implementation.

application.bottlerName: Stone's Throw Brewing Co., Burlington, Vermont

labelText.bottlerName: BREWED AND BOTTLED BY STONE’S THROW BREWING CO., BURLINGTON, VERMONT
labelText.warningBody: (1) According to the Surgeon General, women should not drink alcoholic beverages during pregnancy because of the risk of birth defects. (2) Consumption of alcoholic beverages impairs your ability to drive a car or operate machinery, and may cause health problems.

defects.note: ACCEPTABLE VARIANCE, NOT A VIOLATION. Differs only by letter case and apostrophe codepoint (U+0027 vs U+2019). Expected verdict is pass.

expected.summary: Must be approved. Case folding plus unicode punctuation normalisation makes brand and bottler match exactly.

samples.title: Silver Fox Rye — alcohol content mismatch
samples.description: The application declares 45% Alc./Vol. (90 Proof); the artwork prints 40% Alc./Vol. (80 Proof). The label is internally consistent — the proof figure agrees with its own percentage — so only a comparison against the application catches it. Five percentage points is far outside any tolerance.

application.bottlerName: Silver Fox Distilling Co., Lawrenceburg, Indiana

labelText.bottlerName: DISTILLED AND BOTTLED BY SILVER FOX DISTILLING CO., LAWRENCEBURG, INDIANA
labelText.warningBody: (1) According to the Surgeon General, women should not drink alcoholic beverages during pregnancy because of the risk of birth defects. (2) Consumption of alcoholic beverages impairs your ability to drive a car or operate machinery, and may cause health problems.

defects.note: Label understates the application by 5.0 percentage points. Tolerance for distilled spirits is 0.15 percentage points (27 CFR 5.65).

expected.summary: Alcohol content check must fail: 40% on the label against 45% in the application.

samples.title: Lantern Hill Cellars — warning header in title case
samples.description: Every field matches and the warning wording is verbatim, but the mandated header is set as 'Government Warning:' rather than 'GOVERNMENT WARNING:'. 27 CFR 16.21 requires the header in capital letters, so this fails on capitalisation alone. A word-level text diff of the warning will show NO difference — the defect is purely in letter case, which is why the header case is a separate check.

labelText.bottlerName: PRODUCED AND BOTTLED BY LANTERN HILL CELLARS, DUNDEE, OREGON
labelText.warningBody: (1) According to the Surgeon General, women should not drink alcoholic beverages during pregnancy because of the risk of birth defects. (2) Consumption of alcoholic beverages impairs your ability to drive a car or operate machinery, and may cause health problems.

defects.note: Header set in title case. 27 CFR 16.21 requires 'GOVERNMENT WARNING:' in capital letters. Body wording is untouched.

expected.summary: Warning header capitalisation check must fail; the warning text check must still pass.

samples.title: Black Duck Brewery — reworded government warning
samples.description: The header is correct but the mandated wording has been altered in two places: 'women should not drink' is softened to 'women should avoid drinking', and the closing clause 'and may cause health problems' is dropped from statement (2). The warning text is prescribed verbatim, so any substitution or omission fails. This sample is the one to use when demonstrating the word-level warning diff.

labelText.bottlerName: BREWED AND BOTTLED BY BLACK DUCK BREWERY, PORTLAND, MAINE
labelText.warningBody: (1) According to the Surgeon General, women should avoid drinking alcoholic beverages during pregnancy because of the risk of birth defects. (2) Consumption of alcoholic beverages impairs your ability to drive a car or operate machinery.

defects.applicationValue: (1) According to the Surgeon General, women should not drink alcoholic beverages during pregnancy because of the risk of birth defects. (2) Consumption of alcoholic beverages impairs your ability to drive a car or operate machinery, and may cause health problems.
defects.note: Two deviations from the prescribed wording: 'should not drink' replaced by 'should avoid drinking', and ', and may cause health problems' omitted from statement (2). See labelText.warningBody for the exact printed string.

expected.summary: Warning text check must fail on both a substitution and an omission; header capitalisation still passes.

samples.title: Juniper & Thorne — net contents absent from label
samples.description: The application declares 750 mL but the artwork carries no net contents statement anywhere. The alcohol statement is centred so that nothing appears conspicuously missing to the eye — the omission has to be found by reading the label, not by spotting a gap. This is the sample that separates 'field absent' from 'field unreadable': the field is legibly not there.

labelText.bottlerName: DISTILLED AND BOTTLED BY JUNIPER & THORNE DISTILLING, PORTLAND, OREGON
labelText.warningBody: (1) According to the Surgeon General, women should not drink alcoholic beverages during pregnancy because of the risk of birth defects. (2) Consumption of alcoholic beverages impairs your ability to drive a car or operate machinery, and may cause health problems.

defects.note: No net contents statement is printed anywhere on the artwork. Expected verdict is fail (absent), NOT unreadable — the image is clean and the field is legibly not present. Note also that `containerInfoNotOnLabels` is deliberately left unset on this application: nothing is declared as blown, branded or embossed into the container, so the escape hatch for embossed net contents does not apply and the omission is a genuine failure.

expected.summary: Net contents check must fail as absent from the label. Also exercises an ampersand in the brand name.

samples.title: Compliant bourbon — blurred and underexposed
samples.description: Out of focus and shot in poor light. The brand and class/type survive; the government warning small print does not. This is the sample that should exercise the UNREADABLE path rather than a pass or a fail — the correct behaviour is to decline to judge the warning, not to guess at it. Verified: the reader transcribes every field correctly here, so the expected outcome is approve — this sample tests robustness to poor exposure, not rejection.

samples.title: Old Tom Distillery — warning washed out
samples.description: The artwork is crisp and every field is correct, and the health warning is word-for-word the statutory text. It is simply printed so faintly that nobody would read it. A text-only comparison passes this label; only a legibility judgement catches it. This is the evasion described in discovery — "smaller font... burying it in tiny text".
